reading.rtitle: Before the Curtain Goes Up: How to Read a Night at the Theater
paras: Every Broadway show hands you the same small booklet at the door: the playbill. Most people put it in a bag and look at it once the lights go down, which is too late. A playbill gives you a lot of information in very little space, and the first few pages tell you almost everything you need: the title, the running time, whether there is an intermission, and the names of the cast. Read it in the ten minutes before the curtain goes up, and you will follow much more of the story.

Look for the small white slip of paper inside. It is the most important page of the night, and many people never see it. It tells you that, at this performance, one of the roles will be played by an understudy: an actor who learns the part and waits, sometimes for months, for a night like this one. Do not ask for your money back. Understudies often steal the show, because they have had a lot of time to prepare and very few chances to be seen.

Your ticket tells you where you are sitting, and the words can be confusing. The orchestra is the floor level, closest to the stage, and it costs the most money. The mezzanine is the first balcony, above it: there are fewer seats, the view of the whole stage is often better, and the prices are a little lower. An usher at each door checks your ticket and walks you to your row. If the show is sold out, there is not much room to move, so go to the restroom before you sit down.

Then there is the end, which visitors often get wrong. When the story finishes, the actors come back for the curtain call, one group at a time, and the audience applauds. If the night was special, people stand up: that is a standing ovation, and on Broadway it happens a lot, perhaps too often. Do not leave during the curtain call. And if you go to a matinee, the afternoon performance, you will see something else: fewer tourists, more locals, and a few people who know every song by heart, because the show is a revival of something they first saw thirty years ago.

listenings.text: Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to tonight's performance. Before the curtain goes up, a few quick notes. Please turn off your phones now, not at the intermission, and remember that photos and videos are not allowed at any time during the show. Tonight's performance runs two hours and thirty minutes, with one intermission of fifteen minutes. That is not much time, so if you would like a drink, please order it at the bar in the lobby before the show, and it will be waiting for you at the break. At this performance, the role of Anna will be played by the understudy, Rachel Moore. You will find a small white slip with her name inside your playbill. If you need help finding your seat, especially in the mezzanine, please ask an usher. And finally, tonight's show is sold out, so there are very few empty seats, and no room at all in the aisles. Please keep your bags under your seat. Enjoy the show.

So, we finally went to a show last week. And it was not easy, let me tell you. Every evening performance was sold out for weeks, so I entered the online lottery, and I lost. Three times. Then a friend told me about the matinee on Wednesday afternoons. Fewer tourists, cheaper tickets, and a lot of seats in the mezzanine. So we went on a Wednesday. And when I opened the playbill, there was this little white slip. The lead actress was out, and an understudy was playing the part. And honestly, I was a little disappointed, for about five minutes. And then she started to sing, and she stole the show. At the curtain call, the whole theater stood up. A standing ovation, for an understudy, on a Wednesday afternoon. I have been to a lot of shows, and I had never seen that.

Thank you for calling the box office. Here are the answers to the questions we hear most. Matinee performances are on Wednesdays and Saturdays at two o'clock, and evening performances begin at eight. There are very few seats left for this month, but we still have a little availability on Wednesday afternoons, mostly in the mezzanine. You can buy up to four tickets per person, and not more. If you need a wheelchair space, please tell us when you book, because there are only a few in each performance. We do not give much information about cast changes by phone. If an understudy is going on, you will find the name on a slip in your playbill. And please arrive at least thirty minutes early. Latecomers are seated by an usher at a good moment in the show, and sometimes that means waiting until the intermission.
